kaps_punt: Voedsel wat mense eet - vanaf plante en diere (klassifikasie)

items.bewering: Die kos op jou bord het nie in die winkel begin nie.
items.blok: Kos begin nie in die winkel nie
items.bron: Our World in Data, 'Global land for agriculture' (ourworldindata.org/global-land-for-agriculture): crops supply about 82% of the world's calories and animal products about 18%; all of it is produced (grown, raised or caught) before it reaches a shop.

items.bewering: Die meeste van ons kos word eers op 'n plaas gekweek of grootgemaak.
items.blok: Kos begin nie in die winkel nie
items.bron: Our World in Data, 'Global land for agriculture': crops about 82% of global calories; meat, dairy and farmed fish about 17%; wild-caught fish about 1%. 'Die meeste' is correct; it does not claim all food (wild fish, salt) is farmed.

items.bewering: Party boere kweek plante, party hou diere aan en ander doen albei.
items.blok: Kos begin nie in die winkel nie
items.bron: FAO, mixed crop-livestock systems (fao.org/4/x5478e/x5478e0d.htm) and Thornton & Herrero 2015 (CSIRO, mixed crop and livestock farming systems in sub-Saharan Africa, including South Africa): mixed farming combines crop growing and livestock on one farm; specialised crop and livestock farms also exist.

items.bewering: Ons noem hierdie werk boerdery.
items.blok: Kos begin nie in die winkel nie
items.bron: Standard definitions of agriculture (e.g. 'the science and practice of cultivating soil, growing crops, and raising livestock for food, fiber, and other products'; Wikipedia 'Outline of agriculture'; Britannica 'agriculture').

items.bewering: Daarom kom die meeste van ons kos van plante of van diere af.
items.blok: Kos begin nie in die winkel nie
items.bron: Our World in Data, 'Global land for agriculture' (crop and animal sources supply nearly all calories). The inference holds; 'die meeste' also leaves room for the farmed mushrooms the lesson treats as neither in its last block.

items.bewering: Mielies groei op 'n lang plant met groot blare.
items.bron: Tropical Forages fact sheet 'Zea mays' (apps.lucidcentral.org/tropical_forages): erect annual mostly 2-3 m tall; New World Encyclopedia 'Maize': leaves like broad flags 50-100 cm long and 5-10 cm wide.

items.bewering: Ons eet die pitte wat aan die mieliekop sit.
items.bron: Tropical Forages 'Zea mays' and New World Encyclopedia 'Maize': the ear consists of a cob (rachis) bearing 4-30 rows of kernels, the part eaten; the ear sits on a short stalk in a leaf axil about halfway down the stem. Dictionary of South African English 'mealie' (an ear of maize). The lesson rightly does not place the mieliekop at the top of the plant, which keeps it distinct from wheat in the next sentences.

items.bewering: 'n Appel is die vrug wat aan die takke van 'n appelboom groei.
items.bron: Canadian Food Inspection Agency, 'The Biology of Malus domestica Borkh. (Apple)' (inspection.canada.ca); Kew Plants of the World Online, Malus domestica: a branched deciduous tree whose fruit is the apple (botanically a pome; 'vrug' is correct in everyday and botanical use).

items.bewering: By 'n wortel eet ons die deel van die plant wat onder die grond groei.
items.bron: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Carrot' (britannica.com/plant/carrot): Daucus carota produces an edible taproot; the rosette of leaves develops above ground while the edible carrot is below. Also NParks Flora & Fauna Web, Daucus carota.

items.bewering: Koring is 'n plant met klein korrels bo-aan sy stingel.
items.bron: Britannica Kids, 'wheat' (kids.britannica.com/kids/article/wheat/353923): at the end of the stem is a head, or spike, of 20-100 tiny flowers that produce the kernels.

items.bewering: Die meeste brood word van koring gemaak.
items.bron: DALRRD, Wheat Market Value Chain Profile 2020 (old.dalrrd.gov.za): wheat in South Africa is mainly used for human consumption (bread, biscuits, breakfast cereals, rusks); bread flour milled is overwhelmingly wheat (white 76.6%, brown 16%). Food-science literature: bread is produced mainly from wheat flour because of its gluten; other grains (maize, rye, sorghum) are used in smaller amounts.

items.bewering: Daarom tel brood ook as kos van 'n plant.
items.bron: As above: the main ingredient is wheat flour; breads not made from wheat are made from other grains (maize, rye, sorghum), which are also plants, so the conclusion holds for bread generally. Minor ingredients (yeast, salt) do not change the usual classification by main ingredient.

items.bewering: Melk kom van diere af
items.bron: South African Regulation R.1510 of 2019 (Agricultural Product Standards Act, dairy and imitation dairy products), Table 22 (api.acts.co.za): the legal class designation for imitation milk is '(Name of plant) Milk', so soy, oat, almond and similar drinks are sold in South Africa as milk; coconut milk ('klappermelk') is a common South African cooking ingredient. A learner applying this lesson's own sorting rule to sojamelk or klappermelk would sort it as animal food because the lesson says milk comes from animals.
items.regstelling: Do not say that all milk comes from animals. Narrow it to the milk the lesson means (the milk we usually drink, and the milk that butter and cheese are made from), which comes from animals and in South Africa mostly from cows. The lesson's own point in 'Sorteer self enige kos' (botter and grondboontjiebotter: a name does not tell you where food begins) applies to plant milks too, so the lesson must not contradict it here. Narrow the quantifier; do not cut the true general statement about dairy milk.

items.bewering: in Suid-Afrika veral van koeie
items.bron: DALRRD, Dairy Market Value Chain Profile 2021 (old.dalrrd.gov.za): commercial dairy herd about 1.27 million cows, mainly Holstein and Jersey; DALRRD goat milk agro-processing document: most goats in South Africa are kept for meat and goat milk is not produced in large quantities.

items.bewering: Vleis kom ook van diere, soos beeste, skape en hoenders.
items.bron: DALRRD statistical and BFAP figures as reported (DALRRD SSI report Sep 2019; Farmer's Weekly, 'South Africans hungry for meat and dairy'): per-capita meat consumption in South Africa is chicken, then beef, then pork and sheep meat. All three examples are farmed meat animals; 'soos' leaves room for others such as pigs.

items.bewering: Die eiers wat ons eet, kom meestal van hoenders af.
items.bron: DALRRD, Egg Market Value Chain Profile 2021 (old.dalrrd.gov.za): the South African egg industry is built on a laying flock of about 29 million hens; other eggs (duck, ostrich) are niche, so 'meestal' is accurate.

items.bewering: Kaas groei nie self nie en word deur mense van melk gemaak.
items.bron: Wikipedia 'Cheesemaking' and Britannica Dictionary 'curd' (britannica.com/dictionary): cheese is made by people by coagulating milk (acidifying with a culture and adding rennet) into curds and whey. 'Groei nie self nie' is correct in the sense intended (cheese is not grown like a plant or raised like an animal).

items.bewering: Die melk kom van 'n dier soos 'n koei of 'n bok.
items.bron: Wikipedia 'Cheesemaking'; Britannica Dictionary 'goat cheese': cheese is made from the milk of cows, goats, sheep, buffalo and other mammals. Consistent with the earlier 'veral van koeie' sentence when the block is read as a set.

items.bewering: Daarom is kaas ook kos van 'n dier.
items.bron: As above: cheese is a dairy product made from animal milk; the conclusion follows. (Cultures and rennet substitutes do not change the usual classification by main ingredient.)

items.bewering: Tog lyk dit glad nie soos melk nie.
items.bron: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'cottage cheese' (britannica.com/topic/cottage-cheese) and FAO dairy text (fao.org/4/j2366e/j2366e16.htm): cottage cheese is a fresh, unripened, near-white cheese of soft curds usually mixed with whey or cream. Fresh white cheeses common in South Africa (maaskaas, roomkaas) are white, soft and visibly made of milk curd, so 'glad nie' is too absolute. It is true of the hard yellow cheeses a learner most often sees.
items.regstelling: Minor, but absolute: soften the quantifier so it is not a claim about every cheese (most cheese looks very different from milk), rather than cutting the useful point that you cannot tell where food comes from by looking at it.

items.bewering: Sorteer self enige kos
items.bron: The lesson itself: the block's first sentence says 'Jy kan die meeste kos self in een van hierdie twee groepe sorteer', and the next block, 'Kos wat nie in die twee groepe pas nie', exists because salt and mushrooms do not fit either group (Britannica 'Fungus'; salt is the mineral sodium chloride). A heading is read alone and displayed large; read with this block's two-outcome rule, 'enige' teaches that every food sorts into plant or animal.
items.regstelling: Bring the heading's quantifier in line with the block ('die meeste', not 'enige'), or name the method rather than promising it works for any food, so the heading read alone does not contradict the next block.

items.bewering: Jy kan die meeste kos self in een van hierdie twee groepe sorteer.
items.bron: Our World in Data, 'Global land for agriculture' (crops and animal products supply nearly all calories); exceptions such as salt and fungi are real but few.

items.bewering: Volg die kos terug tot by die plek waar dit begin het. As dit by 'n plant begin, is dit kos van 'n plant. As dit by 'n dier begin, is dit kos van 'n dier.
items.bron: Tested as a method on a common South African food. Honey begins as flower nectar (a plant), which bees collect, transform with their own enzymes and store in the comb (AGES Austria, 'Honey'; SFDA honey consumer guide), yet honey is classed as a product of animal origin, e.g. EU Regulation (EC) 853/2004, Annex I, point 8.1, and is treated as an animal product in vegan practice. This rule, and the lesson's own pattern ('X word van Y gemaak en is dus kos van ...'), sorts honey as plant food. The rule also gives no stopping point: a learner who keeps tracing can take milk or meat back to the grass the cow ate and call them plant food. The rule's worked examples (butter, peanut butter) all sort correctly, and no stated fact is false; the failure is in where the method leads a learner who applies it to the next food.
items.regstelling: Give the rule a stopping point a nine-year-old can apply: trace the food back to the plant or animal that made or gave it (the cow gave the milk, the hen laid the egg), not further back to what that animal ate. Do not settle the honey case by adding honey as a new example; its classification is not something this lesson needs, and any added example needs its own check.

items.bewering: Botter word van melk gemaak en is dus kos van 'n dier.
items.bron: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'butter' (britannica.com/topic/butter): a solid emulsion produced by churning the cream from cow's milk; can be made from whole milk but usually from cream, which is part of milk.

items.bewering: Grondboontjiebotter word van grondboontjies gemaak en is dus kos van 'n plant.
items.bron: US 21 CFR 164.150 (law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/21/164.150): peanut butter is prepared by grinding shelled and roasted peanuts, with added seasoning and stabilisers not exceeding 10% by weight; the peanut (Arachis hypogaea) is a legume crop grown for its seeds.

items.bewering: Die twee name klink amper dieselfde, maar die kos begin by heeltemal verskillende plekke.
items.bron: As the two items above: butter comes from an animal's milk, peanut butter from a plant's seeds. The comparison's mapping is sound (a similar name does not mean a similar origin); peanut butter is called 'butter' for its spreadable texture, not its ingredients. Note that this sound principle is contradicted by 'Melk kom van diere af' in 'Kos van diere' (see that item).

items.bewering: Die meeste kos wat ons eet, pas in een van hierdie twee groepe.
items.blok: Kos wat nie in die twee groepe pas nie
items.bron: Our World in Data, 'Global land for agriculture'.

items.bewering: Party kos pas egter in nie een van die twee nie.
items.blok: Kos wat nie in die twee groepe pas nie
items.bron: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Fungus' (mushrooms and yeasts are kingdom Fungi); salt is a mineral (see next item).

items.bewering: Sout kom uit die see of uit die grond en was nooit 'n plant of 'n dier nie.
items.blok: Kos wat nie in die twee groepe pas nie
items.bron: Mail & Guardian, 'Salt: the journey from mine to meal' (29 January 2015, mg.co.za) and SA Salt Forum 2023 presentation (imformed.com): South African salt comes from seawater evaporation and from underground brine pumped from boreholes at Northern Cape pans, and salt is also mined as rock salt (halite) elsewhere. Salt is the mineral sodium chloride.

items.bewering: Sampioene lyk soos plante, maar hulle is nie plante of diere nie.
items.blok: Kos wat nie in die twee groepe pas nie
items.bron: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Fungus' (britannica.com/science/fungus): mushrooms belong to kingdom Fungi; fungi were historically included in the plant kingdom (hence 'lyk soos plante' is a fair comparison) but were separated because they lack chlorophyll and differ structurally, and they differ from animals in how they grow and take in food. Some dietary guides group mushrooms with vegetables for cooking purposes, but that is a kitchen grouping and does not make the biological claim false.

items.bewering: boerdery: Om plante te kweek en diere aan te hou vir kos en ander produkte.
items.bron: Standard definitions of agriculture ('growing crops and raising livestock for food, fiber, and other products'; Wikipedia 'Outline of agriculture'; Britannica 'agriculture'). Read alone, 'en' lists the activities farming includes, as dictionary definitions do, and does not require a farm to do both; 'ander produkte' (wool, fibre, leather) is correct.

opsomming: Every fact in the lesson checked out, but four things need the writer: 'Melk kom van diere af' is too absolute because South African law and kitchens have plant milks (sojamelk, klappermelk), which contradicts the lesson's own point that a name like botter does not tell you where food begins; the sorting rule 'volg die kos terug' has no stopping point, so it sorts honey as plant food and lets a learner trace milk back to grass; the heading 'Sorteer self enige kos' promises that any food can be sorted, against its own 'die meeste' and the next block; and 'lyk glad nie soos melk nie' is too absolute for white fresh cheeses such as maaskaas. Tested as sets: the plant list and the animal list agree with each other and with the closing exceptions, and the mieliekop is correctly not placed at the top of the plant.
